ALEX: So. Google Search in schools. The policy landed today. Managed Google Workspace accounts — that's the institutional version schools pay for — if administrators turn off generative AI features, they lose access to standard Google Search entirely. A hundred percent of managed school accounts are affected.
JAMIE: Every single one.
ALEX: Every single one. And Google's explanation is that the architecture doesn't allow you to separate them anymore. Search and AI are now one thing.
JAMIE: Which, I'm sorry, is a remarkable sentence from the company that invented the ability to find anything on the internet. "You can't search without the chatbot." Right.
RUFUS: To be fair, they didn't quite say chatbot. They said generative AI features. Which is doing a lot of work in that sentence.
ALEX: Does the distinction matter practically?
RUFUS: It might matter legally. If a school is subject to regulations about what AI tools minors can interact with — COPPA, state-level student privacy laws — then "generative AI features" is a liability category, not a product preference.
JAMIE: Which is exactly why administrators are pushing back. This isn't about schools disliking AI. Some of them have specific legal obligations about what their students interact with.
ALEX: Right. And the choice Google is now giving them is: comply with our bundled product, or lose the research tool your students have used for twenty years.
RUFUS: It's a genuinely uncomfortable position. Because Google Search in a school environment is not really optional anymore. It's infrastructure.
JAMIE: It's the library card.
RUFUS: Yes. And they've just said the library card now comes with a mandatory reading companion that some districts are legally restricted from offering.
ALEX: Okay, here's what I want to push on. Google says the decoupling is technically impossible. Is that credible?
JAMIE: I mean — I want to believe them.
ALEX: I know that look.
JAMIE: I believe them in the same way I believe my laptop when it says it needs to restart to install updates at the worst possible moment. Technically true, but also very convenient.
RUFUS: The honest answer is we don't know. The source is clear that Google cites technical architecture as the reason. But the source does not establish what those constraints actually are. We can't verify whether a modular opt-out was ever designed, or whether it was designed out deliberately.
ALEX: Those are very different things.
RUFUS: Completely different. One is engineering. The other is strategy wearing engineering's coat.
JAMIE: And from a school IT administrator's perspective, it doesn't matter which one it is. The outcome is identical.
ALEX: Okay, picture the IT director at a mid-sized school district. She's got a Workspace admin console open right now. She's got state-level student data privacy requirements she has to satisfy. And Google just told her the toggle she was relying on no longer works the way she thought.
JAMIE: And she's looking at her alternatives — which are, what, Bing? DuckDuckGo? —
RUFUS: Which, in a school environment with existing Google Docs, Google Classroom, Gmail — switching costs are enormous.
JAMIE: That's the real leverage. It's not just Search. It's the whole ecosystem.
RUFUS: Google didn't create that ecosystem lock-in today. But they are using it today.
ALEX: Is there a reading of this that isn't adversarial?
JAMIE: Sure. If Search and AI genuinely are architecturally unified now — if the AI is doing the ranking, the summarization, the disambiguation — then offering a "Search without AI" might actually mean offering something that just doesn't work very well anymore.
RUFUS: That's plausible. And it's also the most convenient possible framing for Google.
ALEX: So both things can be true.
RUFUS: Both things can be true. Modern AI-integrated search may genuinely require the AI layer to function as designed. And Google may have designed it that way knowing it would foreclose easy opt-outs.
JAMIE: The part that gets me is the educators. Teachers who've spent years building research curricula around Google Search are now being told: the tool you built your practice around has changed, without your input, and your only choice is acceptance or exile.
ALEX: And they found out today.
JAMIE: They found out today.
RUFUS: What administrators need to do immediately: audit which AI features are currently enabled in their Workspace accounts, check their state and district obligations on student AI exposure, and find out what the effective compliance date actually is. Because the policy is announced — but the enforcement window matters.
ALEX: And if you're a parent?
JAMIE: If you're a parent, ask your school's IT office what their current settings are. Because as of this morning, that answer may have changed without anyone telling you.
RUFUS: The larger signal here — and I think this is worth sitting with — is that Search is no longer a standalone product. That era is over. What replaces it is still being negotiated. And right now, schools are the negotiating table.

scenes.original:
ALEX: Our second story. Meta announced a twenty-five billion dollar debt offering today. Not equity — debt. Bonds. And the money is specifically earmarked for AI infrastructure: data centers, hardware, the computing capacity to train the next generation of Llama models through 2027.
JAMIE: Twenty-five billion.
ALEX: Twenty-five billion.
JAMIE: That is not a rounding error.
RUFUS: And this is separate from previous capital raises. Bloomberg reported this today as a new, distinct debt offering. Not a repackaging of an earlier announcement.
ALEX: Rufus, take us on location.
RUFUS: Picture a midtown Manhattan conference room, some time this morning. Not a flashy one — the kind with a whiteboard that still has last week's risk models on it. Bloomberg is reporting this from Wall Street, where institutional investors are now sitting with Meta's prospectus and asking each other the question they always ask when a tech giant decides to borrow rather than issue stock: what do they know that makes debt cheaper than equity right now?
JAMIE: Or it's a bet they have to make regardless of the return, because falling behind on compute is an existential risk.
RUFUS: That's the other reading. And both can be true simultaneously.
ALEX: Back to the wider story. Jamie, you were about to say something about Llama.
JAMIE: I want to know what happens if the next Llama model — the one this infrastructure is being built for — doesn't drive proportional revenue. What's the debt service on twenty-five billion?
RUFUS: We don't know the specific rate. Bloomberg notes it's subject to market interest rates and bond pricing conditions. But even at a conservative estimate, you're talking about a significant annual obligation.
ALEX: So Meta is borrowing money, at interest, to build infrastructure, to train a model, that it then gives away as open source.
RUFUS: Llama has been open-weight, yes.
ALEX: That business model continues to confuse me.
RUFUS: The logic is that if Llama becomes the standard — if every enterprise builds on it — Meta controls the ecosystem without controlling the product. The infrastructure around it, the enterprise relationships, the advertising data flywheel — that's where the return lives.
JAMIE: It's a long game.
RUFUS: A very expensive long game.
ALEX: But is twenty-five billion too much debt for that long game?
RUFUS: That depends entirely on two things we don't know: the interest rate they secured, and how quickly AI infrastructure spending translates into measurable competitive advantage. Neither is in the source.
JAMIE: What we do know is that Meta's capital expenditure guidance for 2027 is continuing to increase. This is not a one-time catch-up spend. This is a sustained commitment to being one of the two or three entities that can afford to train frontier models.
ALEX: Which raises the question we keep circling: how many organizations can actually sustain this level of spending?
RUFUS: Fewer than are currently trying. That's what this offering signals. Meta is saying: we can. And by borrowing rather than issuing shares, they're saying it without asking shareholders for permission.
JAMIE: The thing that strikes me is the confidence. Not arrogance — confidence. They're not hedging this. Twenty-five billion is a declaration.
RUFUS: For investors watching from the outside, the indicators to track are Meta's debt-to-equity ratio over the next two quarters and whether their CapEx efficiency reports show any evidence that this infrastructure spend is actually translating into model performance gains. If those two things diverge — high debt, flat capability improvement — that's when the questions get harder.
ALEX: And if they converge?
RUFUS: Then it was the right bet, and the people in that midtown conference room will look very smart.
JAMIE: They already look very comfortable. It's the comfort that worries me slightly.
RUFUS: Heh. It's not a feeling you fight. It's a data point you watch.
JAMIE: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Rufus, can we agree that people need something more useful than another argument about AI?
RUFUS: Certainly. Although I object to the implication that our arguments aren't exquisite. The Ledger offers five focused briefings to help connect news with decisions.
ALEX: That's the point of The Ledger: think about what matters for your work and your team, beyond the headline. The link is in our show notes.
JAMIE: The Ledger. Briefings there, exquisite disagreements here. Right, let's get back to it.

scenes.original:
JAMIE: Our third story is the one I keep wanting to talk about, actually.
ALEX: You have been visibly restraining yourself.
JAMIE: Google DeepMind published a science post today about something called Google Antigravity —
ALEX: Still an extraordinary name.
JAMIE: We'll get there. The post describes an agentic workflow for drug discovery. And the specific claim is this: the system can search thousands of compounds, run something called matched molecular pair analysis, and propose novel drug candidates — specifically rigidified macrocycles, with synthetic routes — in about an hour.
ALEX: Okay. I need a translation on a couple of those.
JAMIE: Matched molecular pair analysis is — imagine you have two molecules that are almost identical, but one of them works as a drug and one doesn't. That analysis tries to understand what structural difference caused that. It's a technique chemists use to figure out why something works, then build something better.
ALEX: And rigidified macrocycles?
JAMIE: Macrocycles are large ring-shaped molecules. Rigidifying them — locking their shape — can make them more effective as drugs because they fit their target more precisely. Designing these is genuinely hard chemistry.
RUFUS: And the claim is that this system does the equivalent of a chemist's multi-week literature review and design iteration in sixty minutes.
JAMIE: Using lung cancer treatments as the example context.
ALEX: What's the catch?
JAMIE: That's a great question and I am going to answer it, but first I want you to just sit with what that speed means. Early drug discovery — the phase where you're generating candidates to test — is typically measured in months. Sometimes years. If this workflow genuinely compresses that to hours, that's not an incremental improvement. That's a different kind of science.
ALEX: Okay. I'm sitting with it. Now what's the catch?
JAMIE: The post is a science demonstration. DeepMind explicitly frames it as a workflow demonstration, not a product launch. There's no information about public access, pricing, or general availability. And critically —
ALEX: Wet labs.
JAMIE: Yes. Everything that happens after a molecule is proposed still has to happen in an actual physical laboratory. Animal studies. Toxicology. Clinical trials. That process is not compressed. The AI is making the sketch faster. The confirmation that the sketch is right takes just as long as it always did.
RUFUS: Which, from an economic standpoint, is still a massive improvement. If you can generate and evaluate ten times as many candidate molecules in the design phase, you increase the probability that one of them survives the full development pipeline.
ALEX: It's not making drug development faster. It's making the starting grid bigger.
RUFUS: Which, over a decade of drug development, compresses expected timelines considerably.
JAMIE: And potentially lowers the cost per approved drug. Because you're wasting fewer resources on candidates that were never going to work.
ALEX: How does the agentic part work? Like, is it autonomously deciding what to try next?
JAMIE: The post says it uses agentic cheminformatics workflows — meaning the system is making sequential decisions about what to search, what to analyze, and what to propose, without a human directing each step. It's not just a search engine for molecules. It's doing some of the reasoning work.
ALEX: So it's closer to a lab assistant than a lookup tool.
JAMIE: That's the framing DeepMind is using. And I think it's the right one. The shift we're watching isn't AI as a chatbot that answers questions. It's AI as a collaborator that runs experiments — even if only computational ones.
RUFUS: There's also the callback to Antigravity. Yesterday we were watching whether Jules capabilities were transitioning into that platform by year end.
ALEX: And now we're seeing what Antigravity is actually doing in the wild.
RUFUS: In a research context, anyway. This is a dated demonstration — November third — which means it's happening now, not as a roadmap promise.
JAMIE: What researchers should watch: does this move from a DeepMind science blog post to something that drug discovery teams outside of Google can actually run? That's the transition that matters. Demo to repeatable lab utility. Those are very different things.
ALEX: And that transition is not established by this post.
JAMIE: Explicitly not. The post does not claim general availability. But it's one of the more concrete examples we've seen of what agentic AI actually looks like in a scientific workflow. Not "AI might help with drug discovery someday." AI doing a specific thing, on a specific problem, with a specific time claim, today.
RUFUS: The economic pressure to make this real is enormous. R&D costs in pharma are staggering. If a credible tool exists that meaningfully accelerates the design phase, the demand from drug development organizations will be substantial.
JAMIE: Which is why I actually want to know if this is the year we stop saying "AI could transform drug discovery" and start saying "here's a workflow that did."
ALEX: We're not there yet.
JAMIE: We're not there yet. But this is the closest thing to a dated, sourced, specific example I've seen that points in that direction.
RUFUS: One hour to a proposed candidate with a synthetic route. The question is what percentage of those candidates survive to preclinical testing. That number would tell us everything. And it's not in the post.
ALEX: Watch for it.
JAMIE: Watch for it.
ALEX: We'll be right back after this.
